newsitem.title: USA: US stocks rocked by rising rates, Dow off two pct.
newsitem.headline: US stocks rocked by rising rates, Dow off two pct.

text.p: Fears that rising interest rates will spell the end for Wall Street's record bull market sent U.S. blue chips tumbling to heavy losses on Thursday.

The Dow industrials ended down 140 points, or two percent, at 6741. The decline was the eighth-largest in New York Stock Exchange history in point terms, but not a top selloff on a percentage basis. The blue chip gauge fell as many as 217 points during the afternoon downdraft.
"The bear just bit us," said Doug Myers, vice president of equity trading at Interstate/Johnson Lane.
U.S. stock markets will be closed on Friday to mark the Good Friday holiday.

The Nasdaq composite sank 1.5 percent, losing 20 points to 1250. Losing issues crushed gainers by a 10-to-three ratio on the New York Stock Exchange, with pre-holiday volume moderately active at about 479 million shares.

Analysts said the mood on Wall Street was further soured by events in Canada, where Toronto's key stock index fell three percent before the exchange was forced to close early due to technical difficulties amid a sell-off in mining company Bre-X Minerals Ltd.
The day's losses brought the Dow down about five percent from its record closing high set March 11 at 7085. The Dow Thursday hit its lowest closing level since January 28.

Analysts said key to the sell-off in stocks was the yield on benchmark 30-year Treasury bond's drive well over the seven-percent mark. The long bond ended off 1-9/32, its yield jumping to 7.09 percent, its highest closing level since 7.11 percent on September 11, 1996.
Above seven percent, bonds become increasingly attractive to stock investors, particularily in a volatile market, analysts said.
"Seven percent and a bit of safety is not a bad idea when there's so much uncertainty ahead," said Alan Ackerman, market strategist at Fahnestock and Co.
Investors on Thursday appeared to become more certain that further interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve were in store for Wall Street.

The view was bolstered by economic data Thursday, including stronger-than-expected February existing home sales. In addition, minutes of the Fed's policy-making committee meeting in February showed a higher-than-expected degree of concern for the U.S. inflation outlook.
The minutes from the meeting were released Thursday.

"If it becomes more and more apparent as the weeks go by that the economic strength is going to be persistent, then we're looking at more rate hikes and a real challenge for the equity market for the first time in a long time," said Charles White, managing director of Avatar Associates.
The Dow ended the week with a loss of 64 points.
Interest-rate sensitive stocks were clipped for the third session in a row following the Fed's short-term interest rate hike Tuesday.
Citicorp shed 2-5/8 to 111, Wells Fargo and Co gave back 9-1/8 to 292, J.P. Morgan & Co Inc dropped 2-3/4 to 102-3/4 and Salomon Inc eased 1-1/8 to 52-1/2.

Quaker Oats Co conceded defeat in efforts to turn around its struggling Snapple beverage unit and agreed to sell it for $300 million -- $1.4 billion less than it paid for the business -- to Triarc Cos Inc, the owner of rival Mistic beverages. Quaker ended up 1/4 to 37-3/4. Triarc rose 1-5/8 to 17-3/8.

Bre-X Minerals Ltd plummeted 9-13/32 to 1-31/32 in Nasdaq trading after the Canadian mining company acknowledged that its gold discovery in Indonesia once thought to be the biggest of the century might be far smaller.

Medical device company Medtronic Inc jumped four to 62-3/8 after the company said its pacemaker business is doing well and the company is aiming for 15 percent compound annual growth in earnings and revenues.
The S&P 500 index fell 16.62 to 773.88.
The Nasdaq Composite fell 19.57 points to 1249.51.
((-- Wall Street desk, 212-859-1730))
